lines.text: You'll want a room. The Judge's room is aired. So is the one the bishop was sick in, but I don't put people in that one.
I'm only passing, I'm afraid.
Everyone's only passing. That's what a coaching house is for.
Noon bell's at twelve. Somebody has to ring it.
Something white went by at dawn and bit me on the ankle. Didn't stop and didn't pay. I've had guests like that.
My mother kept this house, and her mother. Neither of them let a bed go unturned, and I don't see why I should start.
I don't either.
There's a book on the desk inside. Everyone who stopped here wrote in it. You can look, if you wipe your hands first.
The guest book is as thick as a family Bible, and every page of it is full.
Forty years back, in the same hand he writes with now, is Eldwin's name.
Further back there's a column of names, each a lifetime from the next, each with three crossed lines beside it. The last of them has written "bound: up", and never signed out.
He had a good hand.
The stage goes by the river now. Has done for twenty-six years. I'm not simple. I know where the road goes.
Then why ring the bell?
It's noon. What else would I do at noon?
Afternoon. This is Patience. She doesn't care for strangers, and she hasn't made an exception yet.
We turned back at the ford, didn't we. We don't argue with geese.
A goose?
Big grey one, taking tolls. Patience wouldn't look at it.
Three letters for Harlow Bridge, and one for Hardscrabble that nobody wants. We'll get there.
Patience shied at something white in the road this morning. She won't say what it was.
Forty years on this road, and I've never opened a letter.
But you know what's in them.
Most of them. You can tell from the hand. People press harder when it's bad news.
There's one for Obed Thayer at Hardscrabble, from his boy at the ironworks. Postage due on it, a dozen eggs. He's turned me away at the door three times.
Perhaps he doesn't want to read it.
He wants to read it. He doesn't want to pay for it.
Reuben raps a knuckle on the nearest barrel and listens.
Hear that? That's a sound barrel.
A week of barrels and nowhere to send them. Goose won't let a cart across.
So you built a wall.
Seemed to be the custom round here.
My wife went over to market Tuesday. She's still over there. So's the market.
Reuben taps Eldwin's staff, and listens.
Good wood. Bit of a crack near the top. I'd not lean on it.
I've been leaning on it for forty years.
Then it's used to you.
Hepzibah'll be back across by supper. I'd best find where Lem put the plates.
I've been sleeping in the shop. House is too quiet with her gone.
And Lem?
Lem sleeps in the shop too. Says it's to keep me company.
My father made barrels for the coaching house up the road. Every one of them's still sound. Nobody's put anything in them for twenty years.
You have to pay him. It's on the sign.
Pay whom?
The goose. He's a toll keeper really. He's under a spell. If enough people pay, it breaks.
How much have you paid?
All my crusts since Monday.
I did the sign myself. TOLL is the hard word.
He's still a goose.
I'm afraid so.
Then it's the other one. The white one. She's the one who's enchanted.
He's still a goose. I'm keeping the sign anyway.
Pa sleeps in the shop now. I go too, so he doesn't get frightened.
If she turns into a lady, you have to bring her back here. I want to see.
You'll be the first to know.
Three days. That's three marks on the tailboard. I'll make it four if I have to, but I won't be happy about it.
I've tried bread. I've tried cabbage. I sang to it. It took my hat.
If you're thinking of walking straight at it, I did that Tuesday. Ask my shins.
Well. Somebody's done it. It's still got my hat, mind.
It's still got my hat, mind.
It's slate for a church roof at Harlow Bridge. Sixty squares of it. I've never been inside a church.
You'll soon have been on top of one.
That's as close as I need.
I keep the count in chalk so I can wipe it off when I get home. Nobody needs to know how long anything took.
Ninety feet if she's an inch, and not a knot in her. Six thousand board feet, standing there doing nothing.
The pine?
My father wouldn't cut her. His father wouldn't. I'm not going to be the one.
You'd go about four hundred board feet, yourself. Dry.
Somebody cut those marks in her bark before any of us were here. Three lines, crossed. My grandfather said leave her be, and didn't say why.
Did you ask him?
You didn't ask my grandfather things.
My boy's twelve. Next year he'll want to know why we don't cut her, and I'll have nothing to tell him.
Mind the edge! Oh. You're not Gideon.
No.
Thought not. He's louder.
Nothing falls on you down here that you didn't saw yourself.
Haven't seen the sky proper since spring. Gideon tells me about it. Says it's mostly still there.
There's a beaver been at the trees by the pond. Gideon says it's done more work this month than I have. He's not wrong. He didn't have to say it.
You took the long way. Most people do.
I didn't see you on the road.
I came the short way.
There isn't one.
Not for you.
Fire's free. I'll put it on account.
Whose account?
Kettle's boiled. Do you want tea or not?
I don't sell to geese. They don't pay, and they don't forget.
Roads round here are longer than they look. That one more than most.
Longer how?
Mind your feet on the wall stones up there. They're loose.
Gideon offered me the pine, if I could find him a buyer. I said I'd ask around. I won't.
Why not?
Bad for business.
Forty-one. Forty-two. Forty... Forty-two. Should be forty-three.
One short?
One short. Gyp knows which one. Gyp's not saying.
I've walked this wall since I was smaller than the sheep. Never once looked over it.
Never?
No call to. Nothing of mine over there.
Gyp's fourteen. She does the counting now. I only say the numbers out loud so she knows I'm still with her.
Cold comes off that wall, mornings. My father said keep the flock this side of it, and I do. He was usually right about cold.
Patience looks at Eldwin with one eye, then the other, and goes back to thinking about something else.
Gyp gives Eldwin a short look and goes back to watching the flock. She has a job.
The sheep chews, and looks at Eldwin as if he were weather.
The ewe is back with the others, and acting as if she never left.
